claims.source: Other reports have demonstrated that cells containing Huntingtin aggregates display reduced transferrin uptake indicating that endocytosis may be compromised (Yu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2014.

claims.claim: In WT or non-pathogenic HTT Q15 expressing hemocytes, CCSs show centripetal movement.
claims.source: In the WT or non-pathogenic HTT Q15 (data not shown) expressing hemocytes, we observed a centripetal movement of CCSs similar to previous observations (Kochubey et al., 2006; Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kochubey et al., 2006 and by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claims.claim: In HTT Q138 expressing cells there was little to no movement of CCSs.
claims.source: However, in HTT Q138 expressing cells there was little to no movement of these CCSs (Figure 1B; Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1—video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and associated videos.

claims.claim: In WT/HTT Q15 expressing cells, CCSs follow a specific path with defined speeds.
claims.source: Using particle image velocimetry (PIV) analysis (see Materials and methods for details and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to quantify the movement and directionality of CCSs, we determined that in WT/HTT Q15 expressing cells, CCSs follow a specific path with defined speeds (Figure 1A'), whereas CCSs in HTT Q138 expressing cells do not show any directional movement, with negligible radial speed indicating a severe compromise in clathrin dynamics and movement of clathrin-coated structures (Figure 1B').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PIV analysis data shown in Figure 1A'.

claims.claim: CCSs in HTT Q138 expressing cells do not show any directional movement, with negligible radial speed indicating a severe compromise in clathrin dynamics and movement of clathrin-coated structures.
claims.source: Using particle image velocimetry (PIV) analysis (see Materials and methods for details and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to quantify the movement and directionality of CCSs, we determined that in WT/HTT Q15 expressing cells, CCSs follow a specific path with defined speeds (Figure 1A'), whereas CCSs in HTT Q138 expressing cells do not show any directional movement, with negligible radial speed indicating a severe compromise in clathrin dynamics and movement of clathrin-coated structures (Figure 1B').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PIV analysis data shown in Figure 1B'.

claims.claim: HTT Q138 expressing hemocytes showed reduced colocalization of mBSA with CCSs coupled with reduced internalization in comparison to control hemocytes.
claims.source: HTT Q138 expressing hemocytes showed reduced colocalization of mBSA with CCSs coupled with reduced internalization in comparison to control hemocytes (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claims.claim: A loss in movement of CCSs was observed exclusively in the presence of HTT Q138 aggregates in mammalian cells HEK293T and SH-SY5Y, similar to what was observed in hemocytes.
claims.source: We also determined the movement of CCSs in mammalian cells, HEK293T and SH-SY5Y expressing either HTT Q15 or HTT Q138. We observed a loss in movement of CCSs exclusively in the presence of HTT Q138 aggregates, similar to what was observed in hemocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating the existence of similar deficits across cell types and organisms.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The centripetal CCS movement in hemocytes was dependent on the actin cytoskeleton and not on microtubules.
claims.source: Previously using inhibitors such as Latrunculin A, colchicine or nocodazole, it was shown that the centripetal CCS movement in hemocytes was dependent on the actin cytoskeleton and not on microtubules (Kochubey et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kochubey et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The role of the actin cytoskeleton is well established in the context of CME and CCS movement across various mammalian cell lines and in yeast.
claims.source: The role of the actin cytoskeleton is also well established in the context of CME and CCS movement across various mammalian cell lines and in yeast (Meriin et al., 2003; Yarar et al., 2005; Ferguson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meriin et al., 2003; Yarar et al., 2005; Ferguson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Hemocytes treated with Latrunculin A or Cytochalasin D showed severe retardation in CCS movement in comparison to their DMSO treated counterparts.
claims.source: Similar to what was previously reported, we found that hemocytes treated with pharmacological inhibitors of actin polymerization, Latrunculin A (LatA) or Cytochalasin D (CytoD) showed severe retardation in CCS movement in comparison to their DMSO treated counterparts (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Treatment with Latrunculin A or Cytochalasin D was accompanied by a loss of CCSs speed, directionality and centripetal movement.
claims.source: This was also accompanied by a loss of CCSs speed, directionality and centripetal movement (Figure 2A', A'', B' and B'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A', A'', B' and B''.

claims.claim: Actin-GFP was sequestered in HTT Q138 aggregates.
claims.source: To further understand how HTT Q138 impacted actin function, we co-expressed Actin-GFP along with HTT Q138. We observed sequestration of Actin-GFP in the HTT aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There was a dramatic alteration in the dynamics of actin and reduced filopodia number and length in HTT Q138 expressing cells.
claims.source: While we observed a dynamic actin cytoskeleton accompanied by numerous filopodia extensions and retractions in WT/HTT Q15 expressing cells, there was a dramatic alteration in the dynamics of actin and reduced filopodia number and length in HTT Q138 expressing cells (Figure 2C, D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—video 1 and Figure 2—video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and associated videos.

claims.claim: The thickness and intensity of cortical actin was significantly increased in presence of HTT Q138 compared to HTT Q15 expressing cells.
claims.source: Measurement of cortical actin revealed that the thickness as well as intensity was significantly increased in presence of HTT Q138 compared to HTT Q15 expressing cells (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claims.claim: A significant reduction of incorporated actin was observed in HTT Q138 expressing cells, indicating that polymerization of actin was hampered.
claims.source: To study the polymerization of actin in HTT Q15/Q138 expressing cells, we performed barbed end labelling of actin by providing fluorescently tagged actin, similar to what has been previously described (Pardee and Spudich, 1982). A significant reduction of incorporated actin was observed in HTT Q138 expressing cells (Figure 2H I), indicating that polymerization of actin was hampered in the presence of HTT Q138.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H and I, and by citation to Pardee and Spudich, 1982.

claims.claim: There was a reduction in actin flow in hemocytes expressing HTT Q138 compared to WT cells.
claims.source: This was further supported by a reduction in actin flow in hemocytes expressing HTT Q138 compared to WT cells (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: Formation of filopodia requires the activity of the Arp2/3 complex.
claims.source: Formation of filopodia requires the activity of the Arp2/3 complex (Korobova and Svitkina, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Korobova and Svitkina, 2008.

claims.claim: Mass spectrometric analysis of Huntingtin aggregates formed in the brain indicated a sequestration of a number of proteins involved in actin remodeling and endocytosis.
claims.source: Mass spectrometric analysis of Huntingtin aggregates formed in the brain indicated a sequestration of a number of proteins involved in actin remodeling and endocytosis. Among these were components of the Arp2/3 complex, additional actin-modulating proteins, clathrin heavy and light chains and Hip1 and Hip1r, proteins that are known to connect clathrin pits to actin at sites of endocytosis, although the nature of their sequestration and association with aggregates remains unknown (Hosp et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hosp et al., 2017 and Kim et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Significant enrichment of Arp3 was found within HTT Q138 aggregates.
claims.source: Similar to what was previously demonstrated, we found significant enrichment of Arp3, a key component of the Arp2/3 complex within HTT Q138 aggregates (Figure 3A) indicating atleast a partial sequestration of one of the components of the Arp2/3 complex.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Inducing expression of a transgenic Arp3 RNAi construct in hemocytes resulted in a reduction in the number of filopodia along with stalled movement of CCSs and loss of directional movement.
claims.source: Upon inducing expression of a transgenic Arp3 RNAi construct in hemocytes, we observed a reduction in the number of filopodia (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) along with stalled movement of CCSs (Figure 3C and C') and loss of directional movement (Figure 3C'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C, C', C'' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Treatment of wild type cells with CK666, a chemical inhibitor of Arp2/3, resulted in stalled CCS movement.
claims.source: Similar results were also obtained upon treatment of wild type cells with CK666, a chemical inhibitor of Arp2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Profilin in hemocytes resulted in an impairment in CCS movement as well as actin dynamics.
claims.source: Knockdown of Profilin in hemocytes also resulted in an impairment in CCS movement as well as actin dynamics (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Chemical inhibition of Formin by SMIFH2 resulted in stalled CCS movement.
claims.source: Chemical inhibition of Formin, a Rho GTPase involved in regulation of elongation of actin fibers by SMIFH2, also resulted in stalled CCS movement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), further establishing that remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton is required for directional movement of CCSs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Recovery of fluorescence intensity of Clc-GFP was severely compromised in the presence of HTT Q138 compared to an almost complete recovery in wild type and control cells.
claims.source: Recovery of fluorescence intensity of Clc-GFP was severely compromised in the presence of HTT Q138 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) compared to an almost complete recovery in wild type and control (Luc VAL 10) cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Incomplete recovery of Clc-GFP was observed upon knocking down Profilin or upon treatment with Lat A.
claims.source: Incomplete recovery was also observed upon knocking down Profilin or upon treatment with Lat A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The organization and dynamics of microtubules remained unchanged even in the presence of Huntingtin aggregates.
claims.source: We found that the organization and dynamics of microtubules remained unchanged even in the presence of Huntingtin aggregates (Figure 3—videos 1 and 2) supporting the previous finding (Kochubey et al., 2006) that microtubules do not play a role in early events of CME.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—videos 1 and 2, and by citation to Kochubey et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Huntingtin is known to interact with Myosin VI via its optineurin binding domain.
claims.source: Huntingtin is known to interact with Myosin VI via its optineurin binding domain (Caviston and Holzbaur, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Caviston and Holzbaur, 2009.

claims.claim: Myosin VI is implicated in various steps of membrane trafficking and shown to be involved in trafficking of clathrin-coated vesicles.
claims.source: The actin-based cytoskeleton motor, Myosin VI, is also implicated in various steps of membrane trafficking Buss et al., 2001b and shown to be involved in trafficking of clathrin-coated vesicles (Soldati and Schliwa, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buss et al., 2001b and Soldati and Schliwa, 2006.

claims.claim: Myosin VI is associated with CCSs through its C-terminal tail.
claims.source: It has also been shown that Myosin VI is associated with CCSs through its C –terminal tail Buss et al., 2001a.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buss et al., 2001a.

claims.claim: The coordinated action of myosin VI and Clathrin light chain a (CLCa) are essential for the fission of clathrin-coated pits.
claims.source: The coordinated action of myosin VI and Clathrin light chain a (CLCa) are essential for the fission of clathrin-coated pits (Biancospino et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Biancospino et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Knocking down Myosin VI resulted in an impairment of CCS movement.
claims.source: Knocking down Myosin VI, resulted in an impairment of CCS movement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—video 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—video 3.

claims.claim: Knocking down Myosin VI had no discernible effect on actin dynamics or on filopodia formation.
claims.source: However there was no discernible effect on actin dynamics or on filopodia formation (Figure 3—video 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—video 4.

claims.claim: Co-expressing Arp3 along with pathogenic HTT Q138 in hemocytes resulted in a partial restoration of CCS movement and directionality along with filopodia formation.
claims.source: Towards this we co-expressed Arp3 along with pathogenic HTT Q138 in hemocytes and used live cell imaging to check the status of CCS movement and actin dynamics in these cells. We observed a partial restoration of CCS movement and directionality along with filopodia formation (Figure 4A, A', A'' and 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—video 1 and Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, A', A'', 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and associated videos.

claims.claim: Hip1 is one of several proteins involved in the initial stages of Clathrin mediated endocytosis.
claims.source: Huntingtin interacting protein1 (Hip1) is one of several proteins involved in the initial stages of Clathrin mediated endocytosis (Metzler et al., 2001; Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Metzler et al., 2001 and Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Hip1 is a known interactor of Huntingtin protein and expansions in the polyglutamate tract disrupt this interaction.
claims.source: Hip1 is also a known interactor of Huntingtin protein and expansions in the polyglutamate tract, as seen in pathological conditions, are known to disrupt this interaction (Kalchman et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kalchman et al., 1997.

claims.claim: Hip1 is known to interact with actin and the Hip1-actin interaction is known to be regulated by the clathrin light chain.
claims.source: Additionally, Hip1 is also known to interact with actin Senetar et al., 2004 and the Hip1-actin interaction is known to be regulated by the clathrin light chain (Wilbur et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Senetar et al., 2004 and Wilbur et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Hip1 was found to be sequestered in pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates.
claims.source: Further, as previously mentioned, Hip1 was also found to be sequestered in pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates (Hosp et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hosp et al., 2017 and Qin et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Co-expressing Hip1 with pathogenic HTT Q138 resulted in a partial rescue of CCS movement.
claims.source: Upon co-expressing Hip1 with pathogenic HTT Q138, we observed a partial rescue of CCS movement (Figure 4B, B' and B'', and Figure 4—video 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, B', B'' and Figure 4—video 3.

claims.claim: Knocking down Hip1 in wild type hemocytes resulted in a reduction in movement, speed, and loss of directionality of CCSs.
claims.source: Conversely, knocking down Hip1 in wild type hemocytes resulted in a reduction in movement (Figure 4C), speed, and loss of directionality of CCSs (Figure 4C' and C''), thus highlighting the importance of the Hip1- actin axis in CME and its possible disruption in the presence of HTT Q138.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C, C' and C''.

claims.claim: Drosophila Mrj, a homologue of mammalian DnaJB6, was observed to rescue polyglutamine associated toxicity in Drosophila.
claims.source: Previously, Drosophila Mrj, a homologue of mammalian DnaJB6 was observed to rescue polyglutamine associated toxicity in Drosophila.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text without a specific citation in this sentence, but is supported by the broader context.

claims.claim: DNAJB6, a member of the DNAJ (HSP40) chaperone family, was found to efficiently suppress polyQ aggregation in cells.
claims.source: In a screen for polyQ modifiers, DNAJB6, a member of the DNAJ (HSP40) chaperone family was found to efficiently suppress polyQ aggregation in cells (Hageman et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hageman et al., 2010.

claims.claim: PolyQ toxicity and aggregation can be modulated by DNAJ chaperones in mice and Drosophila.
claims.source: Previous studies in mice and Drosophila have also shown that polyglutamine toxicity and aggregation can be modulated by DNAJ chaperones (Labbadia et al., 2012; Warrick et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Labbadia et al., 2012 and Warrick et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Mrj can effectively suppress polyQ toxicity.
claims.source: The DNAJ domain containing protein Mrj, which is highly enriched in the brain, can effectively suppress polyQ toxicity (Chuang et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chuang et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Mrj was identified in an independent screen to modulate the cytotoxicity in the context of protein aggregation.
claims.source: Additionally, Mrj was also identified in an independent screen to modulate the cytotoxicity in the context of protein aggregation (Desai et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Desai et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Coexpressing Mrj along with HTT Q138 in hemocytes partially restored CCS movement, speed and directionality along with filopodia formation.
claims.source: We found that coexpressing Mrj along with HTT Q138 in hemocytes partially restored CCS movement (Figure 4D) speed and directionality (Figure 4D' and D'' and Figure 4—video 4) along with filopodia formation (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D, D', D'', 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—video 4.

claims.claim: Overexpression of either Arp3, Hip1 or Mrj could rescue the neurodegeneration observed in Drosophila eyes caused by the overexpression of pathogenic HTT Q127.
claims.source: Additionally, overexpression of either Arp3, Hip1 or Mrj could also rescue the neurodegeneration observed in Drosophila eyes caused by the overexpression of pathogenic HTT Q127 (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Cells expressing HTT Q138 were stiffer than WT cells, as indicated by the higher Young's modulus.
claims.source: Our results demonstrated that cells expressing HTT Q138 were stiffer than WT cells, as indicated by the higher Young's modulus (or stiffness; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The stiffness of cells expressing pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates was partially rescued upon overexpression of either Hip1 or Mrj.
claims.source: The stiffness of cells expressing pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates was partially rescued upon overexpression of either Hip1 or Mrj (Figure 5A) indicating that partial restoration in actin organization may also rescue stiffness of these cells in addition to CME.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Treatment of CK666 led to a decrease in stiffness of cells compared to DMSO-treated cells.
claims.source: We performed AFM on cells treated with CK666, a inhibitor of the Arp2/3 complex and found that treatment of CK666 led to a decrease in stiffness of cells compared to DMSO-treated cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Cells treated with LatA showed decreased stiffness in comparison to DMSO-treated cells.
claims.source: We also noticed a decreased stiffness of cells upon LatA treatment in comparison to DMSO-treated cells (Figure 5A) suggesting that an altered state of the cytoskeleton was largely responsible for contributing to the increased stiffness observed in the presence of HTT Q138.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: A brief, transient treatment of Lat A to HTT Q138 cells resulted in movement of CCSs at an intermediate time point.
claims.source: We were able to see movement of CCSs in these cells at an intermediate time point (Figure 5B) thereby strengthening the idea that CCS movement requires a dynamic form of the actin cytoskeleton and that HTT Q138 causes the cytoskeleton to be held in a very stiff state.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: In the presence of TDP-43, a significant reduction in CCS movement was observed, similar to what was observed in the presence of HTT Q138.
claims.source: We observed that while Aβ–42–2 x, FUSR521C (FUS), αSynA30P or αSynA53T (Figure 6A and Figure 6—video 1–4) caused no defect in CCS movement, in the presence of TDP-43 we noticed a significant reduction in CCS movement (Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—video 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—video 5.

claims.claim: CCSs moved inwards in all cases except TDP-43 expressing cells, in which movement was completely stalled.
claims.source: Tracking and quantification of CCSs in WT cells and cells expressing mutant proteins revealed that CCSs moved inwards in all cases, except TDP-43 expressing cells, in which movement was completely stalled (Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—video 5), similar to what we observed in the presence of HTT Q138.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—video 5.

claims.claim: The mean instantaneous velocities showed a significant decrease in the presence of TDP-43.
claims.source: This was also supported by analysis of the mean instantaneous velocities, which showed a significant decrease in the presence of TDP-43 (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The uptake of fluorescently tagged mBSA was markedly reduced in the presence of TDP-43 indicative of a reduction in CME.
claims.source: Additionally, the uptake of fluorescently tagged mBSA was markedly reduced in the presence of TDP-43 (Figure 6D) indicative of a reduction in CME.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Recovery of clathrin was severely compromised only in the presence of TDP-43, similar to HTT Q138.
claims.source: Recovery of clathrin was severely compromised only in the presence of TDP-43, similar to HTT Q138, and was indistinguishable from WT in the context of other aggregates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A dramatic reduction in filopodia formation was noticed in the presence of TDP-43.
claims.source: Here again, we saw no significant difference in filopodia formation in the hemocytes expressing Aβ–42–2 x (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—video 1), FUSR521C (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—video 2) or both mutants of α-Synuclein (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—videos 3 and 4), but noticed a dramatic reduction in the presence of TDP–43 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Figure 7—video 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Figure 7—video 5.

claims.claim: Number, length and lifetime of filopodia were compromised in the presence of TDP-43 expressing cells as compared to wild type cells.
claims.source: Number, length and lifetime of filopodia were also compromised in the presence of TDP-43 expressing cells as compared to wild type cells (Figure 7B, C and D), while remaining largely unaffected in the context of other mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B, C and D.

claims.claim: Reduced actin flow was observed in TDP-43 expressing cells in comparison to WT cells and cells expressing other aggregates.
claims.source: Reduced actin flow was also observed in TDP-43 expressing cells in comparison to WT cells and cells expressing other aggregates (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Young's modulus for cells having pathogenic aggregates of Aβ–42–2 x, FUS R521C, α-SynA30P and α-SynA53T remained similar to WT cells.
claims.source: Young's modulus for cells having pathogenic aggregates of Aβ–42–2 x, FUS R521C, α-SynA30P and α-SynA53T remained similar to WT cells (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: The stiffness was altered in case of TDP-43, similar to what was seen in HTT Q138, showing a direct correlation of cell's modulus of elasticity with actin dynamics and CME transport.
claims.source: The stiffness was altered in case of TDP-43, similar to what was seen in HTT Q138, showing a direct correlation of cell's modulus of elasticity with actin dynamics and CME transport.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the AFM data and other observations in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Specific pathogenic aggregates alter the physical properties of cells, by directly impacting actin dynamics and hence the CME process.
claims.source: In our study, we demonstrate that specific pathogenic aggregates alter the physical properties of cells, by directly impacting actin dynamics and hence the CME process (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion of the study and is supported by data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The cells with HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates were observed to have increased Young's modulus compared to WT cells indicating stiffening of cells.
claims.source: The cells with HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates were observed to have increased Young's modulus compared to WT cells indicating stiffening of cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a finding based on AFM data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Recovery of stiffness of the cells upon overexpression of actin binding proteins (Hip1 or Arp3) reverts cells towards the WT.
claims.source: Recovery of stiffness of the cells upon overexpression of actin binding proteins (Hip1 or Arp3) reverts cells towards the WT, providing strong support to our hypothesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a finding based on AFM data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Mechanical response of cells can be used as a biomarker for actin mediated altered cell behavior in the presence of pathogenic protein aggregates.
claims.source: More importantly, our AFM results show that mechanical response of cells can be used as a biomarker for actin mediated altered cell behavior in the presence of pathogenic protein aggregates.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the AFM data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The toxicity caused by pathogenic protein aggregates may be due to a reorganization of other proteins, organelles and cellular pathways rendering them dysfunctional.
claims.source: Further, our results demonstrate that the toxicity caused by pathogenic protein aggregates may be due to a reorganization of other proteins, organelles and cellular pathways rendering them dysfunctional (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Rescuing some of the functions affected by pathogenic aggregates may work towards reducing neurotoxicity even in the continued presence of pathogenic aggregates.
claims.source: Rescuing some of these functions may indeed work towards reducing neurotoxicity even in the continued presence of pathogenic aggregates.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The extent of observed change in CCS speed and directionality varied depending on the mutant protein present, suggesting that specific interactions may be responsible for the phenotype.
claims.source: The extent of observed change in CCS speed and directionality varied depending on the mutant protein present, suggesting that specific interactions may be responsible for the phenotype, rather than merely the physical presence of an aggregate in the cell.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The most drastic changes resulting in a complete block in CCS movement were observed in the context of HTT Q138 and TDP-43.
claims.source: The most drastic changes resulting in a complete block in CCS movement were observed in the context of HTT Q138 and TDP-43.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Alterations in CCS movement correlated with changes in actin dynamics as reflected by changes in filopodia length, lifetimes and actin flow.
claims.source: Furthermore, these alterations in CCS movement also correlated with changes in actin dynamics as reflected by changes in filopodia length, lifetimes and actin flow (Figure 2 and Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the data presented in Figure 2 and Figure 7.

claims.claim: The branching function of Arp2/3 is essential for CME.
claims.source: Together, these indicate that the branching function of Arp2/3 is essential for CME, and that the altered function of Arp2/3 by HTT Q138 aggregates may be one of several possible mechanisms by which CME is inhibited in Huntington's disease.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The altered function of Arp2/3 by HTT Q138 aggregates may be one of several possible mechanisms by which CME is inhibited in Huntington's disease.
claims.source: Together, these indicate that the branching function of Arp2/3 is essential for CME, and that the altered function of Arp2/3 by HTT Q138 aggregates may be one of several possible mechanisms by which CME is inhibited in Huntington's disease.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Overexpressing specific proteins that are sequestered into Huntingtin aggregates may help to reduce the toxic effects of the aggregates.
claims.source: This is in agreement with previously published data which demonstrates that overexpression of specific proteins that are sequestered into Huntingtin aggregates may help to reduce the toxic effects of the aggregates (Hosp et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hosp et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Overexpressing Hip1 and Arp2/3 ameliorates Huntingtin aggregate-induced loss of function and restore cellular processes.
claims.source: Our study suggests that overexpressing Hip1 and Arp2/3 ameliorates Huntingtin aggregate-induced loss of function and restore cellular processes (Figure 8B).

results.result: Pathogenic HTT Q138 aggregates severely impair clathrin-coated structure (CCS) movement and directionality in Drosophila hemocytes and mammalian cells. Live cell imaging with PIV analysis demonstrated that while WT/HTT Q15 cells show centripetal CCS movement with defined speeds, HTT Q138 cells exhibit little to no CCS movement with negligible radial speed and loss of directional movement. This was accompanied by reduced mBSA internalization and was conserved across cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C33-C38 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (kymographs, PIV analysis, ligand uptake assays) across different cell types (Drosophila hemocytes, HEK293T, SH-SY5Y) demonstrating impaired CCS dynamics in HTT Q138. The quantitative PIV analysis and visual data in Figures 1 and supplementary figures provide strong support.

results.result: HTT Q138 aggregates sequester actin and Arp2/3 complex components, leading to disrupted actin dynamics. Actin-GFP was sequestered in HTT Q138 aggregates, and cells showed dramatic alterations in actin dynamics with reduced filopodia number and length, increased cortical actin thickness and intensity, reduced barbed-end actin incorporation, and reduced actin flow. Arp3 was significantly enriched within HTT Q138 aggregates.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C43-C47, C50 are supported by multiple complementary assays including co-localization studies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), live imaging of actin dynamics (Figure 2C-E), barbed-end labeling (Figure 2H-I), cortical actin measurements (Figure 2F-G), PIV analysis of actin flow (Figure 2J), and Arp3 sequestration data (Figure 3A). The convergence of multiple independent measurements strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Pharmacological or genetic disruption of actin polymerization phenocopies HTT Q138-induced CCS defects. Treatment with LatA or CytoD, knockdown of Arp3 or Profilin, or chemical inhibition of Formin all resulted in stalled CCS movement, loss of directionality, and reduced filopodia formation similar to HTT Q138 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C51-C54 demonstrate that multiple independent perturbations of actin polymerization machinery produce similar phenotypes to HTT Q138, supported by kymographs, PIV analysis, and filopodia quantification (Figures 2A-B, 3B-D, supplementary figures). This provides strong evidence that actin dysfunction is central to the HTT Q138 phenotype.

results.result: Overexpression of Arp3, Hip1, or the chaperone Mrj partially rescues CCS movement defects and neurodegeneration caused by pathogenic Huntingtin. Co-expression of these proteins with HTT Q138 restored CCS movement, directionality, and filopodia formation in hemocytes, and rescued neurodegeneration in Drosophila eyes expressing HTT Q127.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C64, C69, C76-C77 are supported by live imaging data showing restored CCS dynamics (Figure 4A-D), filopodia quantification (Figure 4E), and eye phenotype rescue (Figure 4F). The rescue experiments provide strong evidence for the mechanistic role of these proteins. However, the rescues are described as 'partial,' which appropriately acknowledges incomplete restoration.

results.result: Hip1 knockdown in wild-type hemocytes impairs CCS movement, speed, and directionality.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 is supported by kymograph and PIV analysis data (Figure 4C, C', C'') showing that Hip1 knockdown phenocopies aspects of HTT Q138, providing loss-of-function evidence complementing the overexpression rescue experiments.

results.result: HTT Q138 expressing cells display increased cellular stiffness in an actin-dependent manner, which can be rescued by overexpression of Hip1 or Mrj or by LatA treatment. AFM measurements showed HTT Q138 cells had higher Young's modulus than WT cells, and this stiffness was partially rescued by Hip1 or Mrj overexpression. Treatment with CK666 or LatA decreased cellular stiffness.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C78-C81 are supported by AFM nanoindentation measurements (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The data show consistent increases in Young's modulus with HTT Q138 and rescue with actin-modulating interventions. The methodology appears sound with appropriate controls and statistical analysis.

results.result: Transient LatA treatment of HTT Q138 cells restores CCS movement at intermediate time points.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C82 are supported by kymograph data (Figure 5B) showing that brief LatA treatment can restore CCS movement in HTT Q138 cells. This elegant experiment supports the 'Goldilocks' hypothesis that CCS movement requires an intermediate, dynamic actin state.

results.result: TDP-43 aggregates cause defective CME and stalled CCS movement similar to HTT Q138. Among multiple pathogenic aggregates tested (Aβ42, FUS, αSynA30P, αSynA53T, TDP-43), only TDP-43 showed significant reduction in CCS movement with complete stalling, reduced mean instantaneous velocities, reduced mBSA uptake, and compromised clathrin recovery in FRAP experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C83-C87 are supported by systematic comparison across multiple aggregating proteins using kymographs, particle tracking, velocity analysis (Figure 6A-C), mBSA uptake (Figure 6D), and FRAP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The specificity of the TDP-43 phenotype strengthens the conclusion that not all aggregates affect CME through the same mechanism.

results.result: TDP-43 aggregates dramatically reduce filopodia formation and actin dynamics. TDP-43 expressing cells showed reduced filopodia number, length, and lifetime, as well as reduced actin flow, while other aggregates (Aβ42, FUS, αSyn mutants) had no significant effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by quantitative analysis of filopodia parameters (Figure 7A-D) and PIV analysis of actin flow (Figure 7E). The specificity for TDP-43 parallels the CCS movement data, providing consistent evidence for a shared mechanism between HTT Q138 and TDP-43.

results.result: TDP-43 aggregates increase cellular stiffness similar to HTT Q138, while other pathogenic aggregates do not. AFM measurements showed that cells with Aβ42, FUS R521C, αSynA30P, or αSynA53T aggregates had Young's modulus similar to WT, while TDP-43 cells showed increased stiffness comparable to HTT Q138.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92, C94 are supported by AFM data (Figure 8A) showing selective stiffness increases only with HTT Q138 and TDP-43. This provides strong evidence for a direct correlation between altered actin dynamics, CME defects, and cellular stiffness for these specific aggregates.

results.result: FRAP analysis reveals compromised clathrin light chain exchange in HTT Q138 cells and upon actin perturbation, but not in microtubule disruption. Recovery of Clc-GFP fluorescence was severely compromised in HTT Q138, Profilin knockdown, and LatA treatment, while microtubule organization remained unchanged in HTT Q138 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by FRAP data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and live imaging of microtubules (Figure 3—videos 1-2). The FRAP experiments provide mechanistic insight into how HTT Q138 affects clathrin dynamics, and the microtubule data appropriately rule out this cytoskeletal component.

results.result: Myosin VI knockdown impairs CCS movement but does not affect actin dynamics or filopodia formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by kymograph data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—video 3-4) showing that Myosin VI affects CCS movement independently of actin dynamics. This helps dissect the relative contributions of different motor proteins versus actin organization.

results.result: The study demonstrates that specific pathogenic aggregates (HTT Q138 and TDP-43) alter cellular physical properties by impacting actin dynamics and CME, and that rescuing these functions can reduce neurotoxicity. The mechanical response can serve as a biomarker for actin-mediated altered cell behavior, and toxicity may result from reorganization of proteins and cellular pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C93, C95-C98 represent the major conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. These are well-supported by the convergence of CCS dynamics, actin organization, stiffness measurements, and rescue experiments across the manuscript. The biomarker claim (C96) is appropriately framed as a conclusion from the AFM data.

results.result: The extent of CCS and actin defects varies by aggregate type, with HTT Q138 and TDP-43 causing the most severe effects. The branching function of Arp2/3 is essential for CME, and altered Arp2/3 function by HTT Q138 may be a mechanism of CME inhibition in Huntington's disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 synthesize the comparative analysis across aggregates and the Arp2/3 mechanistic data. The specificity of effects is well-documented (Figures 6-8), and the Arp2/3 mechanism is supported by sequestration data, knockdown/inhibition experiments, and rescue experiments. Claim C103 appropriately uses 'may be' to indicate this is one possible mechanism.

results.result: Overexpressing Hip1 and Arp2/3 ameliorates Huntingtin aggregate-induced loss of function. Previous work shows tight correlation between Hip1R/Arp2/3 availability and endocytic efficiency, with Hip1R distribution regulating recruitment of Arp2/3 complexes.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by the rescue experiments in the current study (Figure 4, Figure 8B). Claims C106-C107 cite prior work (Akamatsu et al., 2020) to provide mechanistic context. The integration of current and prior findings is appropriate.

results.result: The ratio of branching to capping proteins regulates actin network stiffness, with stiffness increasing as either concentration increases. Network stiffness depends on balancing branching and capping, and alterations may affect stiffness and endocytic efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 cite prior in vitro work (Pujol et al., 2012) to provide theoretical framework for interpreting the stiffness results. The citation appears accurate and the interpretation (C110) is reasonable based on the cited work and current findings.

results.result: Clathrin exchange between membrane-associated and soluble pools is compromised in HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 cites prior FRAP studies (Wu et al., 2001; 2003) establishing clathrin exchange. Claim C112 interprets the current FRAP data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) in this context. The conclusion is well-supported by the FRAP experiments.

results.result: CME changes in HTT Q138 and TDP-43 may be actin-dependent, whereas other aggregates may use different mechanisms. Prior work showed that loss of CME in embryonic stem cells alters actin organization and increases stiffness, consistent with the current findings linking mechanical response to altered actin organization in HTT Q138 and TDP-43.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is a reasonable interpretation of the aggregate comparison data. Claim C114 cites prior work from the authors' lab (Mote et al., 2020). Claim C115 synthesizes current AFM and actin dynamics data. The logic connecting these claims is sound.

results.result: The branched actin network generates force for cellular processes including endocytosis, and a 'Goldilocks' intermediate dynamic state is required for efficient CME—neither too soft nor too stiff.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 cites prior work on actin force generation (Goode et al., 2015; Lacy et al., 2018; Planade et al., 2019). Claim C117 represents a key conceptual conclusion from the stiffness and rescue experiments, particularly the transient LatA treatment (Figure 5B). This 'Goldilocks' model is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Rescue of Huntingtin-driven neurodegeneration by actin binding protein overexpression indicates that actin cytoskeleton remodeling contributes largely to aggregate-driven neurotoxicity. The conservation of CCS movement phenotypes across cell types and organisms suggests potential for screening molecular candidates for Huntington's disease.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is supported by the eye rescue experiments (Figure 4F) combined with the mechanistic data on actin. Claim C119 is supported by the conservation of phenotypes across Drosophila hemocytes, HEK293T, and SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). Both conclusions are well-justified.
